<reason>This was a genuinely close, well-matched debate. B grounded its case in concrete anchors (Volcker vs. 2022-24 disinflation, the arbitrariness of the 2% target) and repeatedly forced A to concede that neither entrenchment nor a benign exit is guaranteed, then used that concession as leverage. But A's core "cumulative damage" framework proved more durable across rounds: it conceded tolerance is fine when disinflation is already working, isolating the real dispute to persistent-inflation cases, and it answered B's pressure question with an actual operational stopping rule (tighten once inflation stalls and current policy no longer supports convergence) rather than dodging it. Crucially, A's final closing exposed a real equivocation in B's decisive "tie-breaker goes to reversible harm" claim: that reversibility premise only holds if tolerance actually avoids recession, but in the contested tail-risk scenario it doesn't, it merely stacks inflation losses on top of an eventual downturn. B never got to answer this because A held the last chronological word, leaving a live, unrebutted route for A. B's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost that trimmed its distributional argument (though later restated in rebuttal). On balance A's tighter, more adaptive logical structure and the unanswered final rebuttal give it a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's closing rebuttal (A5.1) against B's "tie-breaker goes to reversible harm" claim, showing that reversibility only applies to the case B already conceded (tolerance without eventual recession), not the contested persistent-inflation scenario where costs stack rather than fade.</best_rebuttal>
